tutorial.step1_text: Start by adding a high-level industrial process block for your facility using the 'Add Process' button.
tutorial.step2_text: Place your process geographically on the interactive map so you can visually plan piping and spatial constraints.
tutorial.step3_text: Break your process down into subprocesses and enter the thermodynamic stream data (Temperature and Mass Flow) for each component.
tutorial.step4_text: Review all the streams you've entered and select which ones you want to include in the potential analysis.
tutorial.step0_text:
Welcome to HeatTransPlan! This tool helps industrial facilities discover energy savings. Here is how the workflow is structured:

1) Data Collection & Facility Mapping
• Start by adding your main operational Processes.
• Break those down into specific Subprocesses (e.g., 'Cooling Tower', 'Boiler').
• For each subprocess, define the individual energy Streams (hot and cold). You must specify the Mass Flow, Heat Capacity (Cp), and the Input/Output Temperatures.
• Use the interactive Map to place your processes geographically, exactly where they are located in your real facility. This helps visualize spatial constraints for future pipe routing.

2) Potential Analysis & Heat Integration
• Review the Stream Summary table to ensure your thermodynamic data is correct.
• Select the specific streams you want to analyze.
• Run the Pinch Analysis to automatically generate Composite Curves. These graphs visually demonstrate your absolute maximum heat recovery potential and identify your 'Pinch Point'.
• Finally, explore Heat Pump Integration to bridge remaining temperature gaps using proposed real-world heat pump models (showing kW and COP parameters).

Click 'Next' to see a visual walkthrough of these steps!

status_quo.title: 📊 Comparison of Status Quo and Proposal
status_quo.desc: Compare the current external energy supply with the absolute minimum external energy required after maximal internal heat recovery (the proposal). Savings indicate how much external utility is avoided.

recovery.title: Heat recovery before integration
recovery.explanation_with: Net load curves — the pocket-free Grand Composite Curve split into a source and a sink profile. Heat is recovered wherever the temperatures allow it, so the heat pump only covers the utility demand that is left over. This is standard pinch practice and the recommended default.
recovery.explanation_no: Composite curves — hot and cold composite curves used directly as source and sink profiles. Internal heat recovery is not assumed, so the heat pump meets the full heating and cooling demands where possible.

stream_selector.title: Streams Selection
stream_selector.help_desc: Select which streams (heat sources or sinks) to include in the pinch analysis. Deselect streams that are currently inactive or should be excluded.

energy_demands.title: Current energy supply
energy_demands.help_desc: Define the baseline energy consumption (heating and cooling) for the selected streams. This represents the 'status quo' before heat integration.

optimization.tooltip_refrigerant_type: Classification of the refrigerant. Natural refrigerants (like Ammonia, CO2) have low environmental impact (GWP) but may have toxicity/flammability considerations. Synthetic refrigerants (like HFCs/HFOs) are traditionally used but often face strict regulations due to environmental impact.
optimization.tooltip_cop: Coefficient of Performance (COP): The ratio of useful heating or cooling provided to work (energy) required. Higher COP means greater efficiency.
optimization.tooltip_q_sink: Heat capacity delivered to the sink (the amount of heat the heat pump provides to the process).
optimization.tooltip_q_source: Heat capacity extracted from the source (the amount of heat the heat pump absorbs from the process or environment).
optimization.tooltip_temp_sink: The target temperature at which heat is delivered to the sink.
optimization.tooltip_temp_source: The temperature at which heat is extracted from the source.
optimization.tooltip_refrigerant: The specific chemical refrigerant used in the heat pump cycle.
optimization.tooltip_hp_stages: The number of compressors (compression stages) in the heat pump system. More compressors can improve efficiency across large temperature lifts.

panel.title: Integration with Heat Pump model and optimization
panel.instruction: Click on any column header to sort. Click on any point in the chart to inspect its details and add it to the table.

filters.source_limited_desc: These cover only part of the demand above T_sink, so they lie off the sink profile.
filters.demand_limited_desc: These cover the full demand but leave waste heat unused at T_source, so they lie off the source profile.
filters.cop_model_desc: 2 temps: source return and sink supply. 4 temps: also source supply and sink return, both taken from the pinch (pinch − ΔTmin/2 and pinch + ΔTmin/2).
filters.custom_cop_desc: Paste a custom COP to perform integration and optimization with your own heat pump.
filters.show_theoretical_desc: Carnot and the best technology archetype, as reference points against the modelled machines.

optimization.desc_actual_source_temp: The real (non-shifted) waste-heat temperature: the shifted temperature + ΔTmin/2.
optimization.desc_shifted_source_temp: The shifted temperature on the Grand Composite Curve. This is the temperature used for the COP calculation.
optimization.desc_actual_sink_temp: The real (non-shifted) process temperature: the shifted temperature − ΔTmin/2.
optimization.desc_shifted_sink_temp: The shifted temperature on the Grand Composite Curve. This is the temperature used for the COP calculation.
optimization.desc_model_information: Please note that the Heat Pump model provided by Copeland is based on physical simulations and yields approximations intended for reference purposes only. For precise calculations or project-specific data, please contact Copeland directly.
optimization.desc_medium_sink: The sink medium for this integration
optimization.desc_hp_simulates: Simulates the integration of various heat pump types to upgrade waste heat from below the pinch to satisfy demands above the pinch, further reducing external utility consumption.
optimization.desc_hpi_chart_p1: Visualizes how a heat pump bridges the temperature gap to lift heat from
optimization.desc_hpi_chart_p2: The solid diamonds represent the heat pump source, and hollow diamonds represent the sink.
optimization.desc_hpi_chart_p3: Heat pumps reduce both external heating and cooling demands simultaneously.
optimization.desc_gcc_chart_p1c: (the bottleneck where the curve touches the Y-axis at Enthalpy = 0).
optimization.desc_gcc_chart_p2: Pockets in the curve (where it moves right then left) show where heat can be cascaded internally without external utilities.
optimization.desc_gcc_chart_p3: The top-right and bottom-right edges show the remaining external hot and cold utility targets.
optimization.desc_cc_chart_p1c: between the Hot (Red) and Cold (Blue) lines represents the maximum heat that can be recovered internally.
optimization.desc_cc_chart_p2: The remaining gaps on the left and right show the external heating and cooling utility we still need to provide.
optimization.desc_cc_chart_p3: The vertical distance between the curves represents the temperature difference driving the heat transfer.
optimization.desc_opt_chart_p1: Visualizes all feasible heat pump solutions based on the predictive model.
optimization.desc_opt_chart_p2: Solid diamonds represent the source points, and open diamonds represent the sink points. Colors correspond to the refrigerant used.
optimization.desc_opt_chart_p3: The large highlighted points indicate the optimal solution or the one you actively clicked on.
optimization.desc_hr_toggle: Chooses how much internal heat recovery is credited before the heat pump is placed. It changes the source and sink profiles that both the heat pump integration and the refrigerant optimization run on, and therefore the resulting duties and COPs.
optimization.desc_opt_chart_invalid: Invalid (violates max condensation temp or pressure limits)
optimization.desc_opt_panel_c1: By default every heat pump above gets its COP from a data-driven model trained based on simualtion data. Here you can add
optimization.desc_opt_panel_c3: as one extra heat pump, so it appears in the same table and chart and can be compared against the model directly.
optimization.desc_opt_panel_c4: Write COP as an expression of the operating temperatures. Available variables:
optimization.desc_opt_panel_c7: — T_sink in K, divided by T_lift
optimization.desc_opt_panel_c8: So a heat pump at 50 % of Carnot is written as
optimization.desc_opt_panel_c15: The formula is checked as you type and previewed at one operating point. Set a
optimization.desc_opt_panel_c17: to say where your heat pump may be used — outside it the pump is not offered, exactly as a model refrigerant is ignored outside its trained range.
optimization.desc_opt_chart_blue_3: represents the total heating demand of your process at each temperature level. The further to the right on the x-axis, the more total heat (kW) is required.
optimization.desc_opt_chart_red_3: represents the total waste heat available to be recovered.
optimization.desc_opt_chart_aims_1: A normal heat pump solution aims to cover the entire sink demand at its delivery temperature. Therefore, its sink point (open diamond) will sit exactly
optimization.desc_opt_chart_why: Why are some points off the blue line?
optimization.desc_opt_chart_off_1: Points plotted to the left of the solid blue line are
optimization.desc_opt_chart_off_3: . This means the available waste heat (red line) is not enough to cover the
optimization.desc_opt_chart_off_5: heating demand required by the process at that specific temperature.
optimization.desc_opt_chart_rest: The heat pump can only supply a portion of the total demand, so it is plotted at a smaller kW value. The rest of the heat will still need to be supplied by an external utility.
optimization.theoretical_hint: A technology archetype from published regressions, not a specific machine. Shown as a reference against the modelled refrigerants.
optimization.real_hint: A regression over heat pump simulation data from a manufacturer parameter study, covering refrigerants, sink media and compression stages, and evaluated here at this point's temperatures.
optimization.carnot_hint: The Carnot relation between the two temperatures, taken at 50 % efficiency as a rule-of-thumb for an achievable heat pump. Not a machine and not a fitted correlation, so a real machine can score above this line.
optimization.entry_type_hint: Real rows are regressions over heat pump simulation data from a manufacturer parameter study, evaluated at each point's temperatures. Theoretical rows are reference points: technology archetypes from published correlations, plus Carnot, which is the thermodynamic relation between the two temperatures at 50 % efficiency.
optimization.tooltip_w_el: The electrical power the compressor draws. It closes the energy balance: P_el = Q_sink − Q_source, which is also Q_sink / COP. A higher COP means the same delivered heat costs less electricity.
optimization.hp_box_what: The pump lifts waste heat from the source profile up to the sink profile.
optimization.hp_box_source: waste heat drawn from the process at that temperature
optimization.hp_box_sink: heat delivered to the process at that temperature
optimization.hp_box_cop: heat delivered per unit of electricity
optimization.cop_coverage_help_1: A heat pump only serves the demand above its sink temperature. Sitting low on the sink profile means covering a small share of the total — but over a short temperature lift, which is cheap, so the COP is high.
optimization.cop_coverage_help_2: Pushing coverage towards 100 % forces the sink temperature up, the lift grows, and the COP falls. The line is the best COP available at each coverage level; everything below it is a worse machine for the same job.
optimization.cop_coverage_help_3: There is no single right answer. A high-COP pump covering 30 % leaves the rest to utility, while full coverage costs more electricity per unit of heat — the choice depends on what that remaining utility costs you.
optimization.hover_demand_limited: demand-limited: waste heat left unused at this temperature

help.title: Analysis Guide
help.smart_selection_desc: Drag an area on the map to batch select streams. Red bubbles are Hot streams (waste heat), Blue bubbles are Cold streams (heat demand).
help.scenarios_desc: Save different project versions (e.g., "Night Shift" vs "Day Shift") as Scenarios to compare their energy performance side-by-side.
help.composite_curves_desc: The horizontal overlap between the Hot and Cold lines represents the heat we can recover. The remaining gaps show the external energy we still need to pay for.
help.grand_composite_curve_desc: Identifies the "Pinch Point" (the bottleneck). Pockets in the curve show where heat can be swapped internally without needing a heat pump.
help.hpi_desc: The system automatically selects the highest-efficiency heat pump for your temperatures. Higher COP values mean better electricity-to-heat conversion.
help.metrics_desc: Heating Savings: The percentage of energy saved compared to your current status quo. Aim for high recovery first!
help.tip: Tip: Use the "Report" button to generate a full PDF-ready dashboard with all your interactive charts.

metrics.min_heating_desc: The absolute minimum external heat required by the system to reach target temperatures after all possible internal heat recovery is utilized.
metrics.min_cooling_desc: The absolute minimum external cooling required by the system after all possible internal heat recovery is utilized.
metrics.pinch_temp_desc: The temperature level dividing the system into a heat sink (above pinch) and a heat source (below pinch). No heat should be transferred across the pinch.
metrics.heat_recovery_desc: The total amount of heat that can be recovered internally by matching hot and cold streams.

economics.title: Economic analysis
economics.empty: Select one or more heat pumps in the table above to compare them economically.
economics.help_1: Net present value method (VDI 2067-1): NPV = −(1 − funding)·I + Σ (CF(t) − R(t))/(1 + i)^t + RV/(1 + i)^T, with CF(t) = reference cost(t) − heat pump cost(t). Fuel, CO₂ and electricity prices rise each year by their own rate.
economics.help_2: Reference (current situation): the chosen heater supplying the largest demand of the selected pumps, plus the cooling that removes the source waste heat today (actively cooled share). Heat or cooling a pump does not take over stays on the old systems. Heat pump electricity = Q / COP × full-load hours.
economics.help_3: Payback is the first year the net present value turns positive (searched up to 40 years). ROI = net present value / net investment (assumed definition).

inputs.pDemand: Capacity charge (if not in electricity price)
inputs.coolShare: Actively cooled share of the source
inputs.eer: Cooling COP of the current cooling (EER)

charts.sens_title: Sensitivity: net present value by {{fuel}} and electricity price ({{funding}} % funding)
charts.time_title: Net present value over time at {{fuel}} {{gas}} ct / electricity {{el}} ct
charts.size_title: Net present value by heat pump size (rest from the {{ref}})
charts.size_x: Heat pump heat output (of {{q}} kW demand)
charts.invest_share: Investment = {{pct}} % of the total costs over {{T}} years

economics.help_4: Investment = specific investment × heat output; the two fields are linked. Literature range for industrial high-temperature heat pumps: about 200–1,500 €/kW, at least ~600 €/kW for lifts above 100 K. Default: 850 €/kW (midpoint).

terms.Q: heat delivered by the heat pump [kW]
terms.Q_ref: heat demand of the reference heater (current situation) [kW]
terms.COP: coefficient of performance of the heat pump [-]
terms.P_el: electrical power of the heat pump [kW]
terms.E_el: electricity consumption of the heat pump per year [kWh/year]
terms.K: operating costs in year t: fuel incl. CO₂ + electricity + maintenance + capacity charge [€/year]
terms.p_0: prices in the base year: fuel excl. CO₂ and electricity [ct/kWh; ÷ 100 for €/kWh in the formula]
terms.r: price change rates per year, separate for fuel, CO₂ and electricity [-]
terms.f_W: maintenance per year as share of the investment [-]
terms.CF: cash flow in year t: cost of the reference minus cost with the heat pump [€]
terms.p_el_star: electricity price at which the heat pump and the reference cost the same over the period, at today's fuel price [ct/kWh]. Cheaper electricity → the heat pump is better
terms.E_fuel: fuel consumption per year [kWh/year] (ref = old heater alone, HP = heat the pump does not cover)
terms.E_cool: electricity of the current cooling per year [kWh/year] (HP = source heat the pump does not take)
terms.Q_src: heat the pump draws from the source = cooling it provides [kW]
terms.Q_src_ref: source waste heat the reference has to cool [kW]
terms.a: share of the source heat that is actively cooled today [-]
terms.EER: cooling COP (EER) of the current cooling: kW heat removed per kW electricity [-]
terms.c_CO2_el: CO₂ factor of grid electricity [t/MWh] (emissions only, its cost is in the electricity price)
terms.p_CO2: CO₂ price in the base year [€/t]; not added for the electric boiler
terms.p_L: capacity charge on the heat pump's electrical power [€/kW per year]
terms.R: reinvestment: share of I in the chosen year, else 0 [€]
terms.RW: residual value after T years, linear depreciation [€]
terms.f_B: operating funding per kWh of heat from the heat pump [€/kWh]
terms.t_B: years the operating funding is paid [years]

economics.roi_assumption: Assumed definition: the presentation shows ROI values but not the formula.
economics.sens_click: The dot is the fuel and electricity price currently used. Hover over a cell for its net present value; click to use that price pair everywhere.

groups.cooling: Cooling the heat pump takes over

input_help.refType:
The system the heat pump replaces, today supplying the heat demand.
Gas boiler: η 90 %, 6 ct/kWh, 0,201 t CO₂/MWh. Oil boiler: η 88 %, 8 ct/kWh, 0,266 t/MWh. Electric boiler: η 99 %, 13 ct/kWh, no extra CO₂ cost (it is in the electricity price).
Picking one fills in efficiency, price and CO₂ factor; all stay editable.
input_help.year:
Year the heat pump starts operating. Year 0 of the net present value: the investment is paid here, savings start the year after.
It only labels the time axis; it does not change the result.
input_help.hours:
Full-load hours per year: how long the heat pump runs at its full heat output.
8.760 h = all year (100 %). Typical: 3.000–6.000 h for one or two shifts, 7.000–8.500 h for continuous processes.
Enters every energy amount: E = Q · h.
input_help.i:
Discount rate: the return the company expects from its money. Future cash flows are divided by (1 + i)^t.
Typical: 4–8 % for industry; it includes inflation. Higher i → future savings count less → lower net present value.
input_help.T:
Period of the analysis in years.
15 years is common for heat pumps: long enough without major reinvestment. The net present value counts cash flows up to T; the payback chart looks further, up to 40 years.
input_help.eta:
Efficiency of the reference heater: heat delivered per kWh of fuel.
Typical: gas boiler 85–95 % (condensing up to ~98 %), oil boiler 85–90 %, electric boiler ~99 %.
Fuel use = Q · h / η.
input_help.pFuel:
Price of {{fuel}} in the base year, without the CO₂ cost, in ct/kWh.
The CO₂ cost is added separately (CO₂ factor × CO₂ price), so do not count it twice. Example: 6 ct + 0,201 t/MWh × 55 €/t = 7,1 ct/kWh in total.
input_help.rFuel:
How much the {{fuel}} price (without CO₂) changes per year, in %.
3 %/year as on the slides. Negative values are allowed (falling prices).
input_help.co2Fuel:
CO₂ emitted per MWh of {{fuel}} burnt, in t/MWh.
Natural gas 0,201, heating oil 0,266 (BAFA/GEG values). Used for the CO₂ cost and the CO₂ rows.
input_help.co2Price:
CO₂ price in the base year, in €/t, added on top of the fuel price.
Germany: national CO₂ price (BEHG) 55 €/t in 2025, 55–65 €/t corridor in 2026; from 2027/28 EU ETS 2. Set 0 if your fuel price already includes it.
CO₂ cost per kWh = CO₂ factor / 1000 × CO₂ price.
input_help.rCo2:
How much the CO₂ price rises per year, in %.
CO₂ prices are expected to rise faster than the fuel itself as the cap tightens; 5 %/year is an assumption, not a forecast.
input_help.pEl:
Electricity price in the base year, in ct/kWh, as paid by the site (energy, grid fees, levies, taxes).
Used for the heat pump and for the cooling electricity it saves. The sensitivity heatmap varies this price.
input_help.rEl:
How much the electricity price changes per year, in %.
The industrial electricity price relief (2026–2028) and grid fee subsidies may lower it short term; 0 to −1 %/year is a reasonable base case, 3 %/year matches the slides.
input_help.co2El:
CO₂ emitted per MWh of grid electricity, in t/MWh. Only for the CO₂ rows; the cost is already in the electricity price.
0,352 = German grid mix (UBA 2025, location-based, slide 29). 0 for a green power contract (PPA).
input_help.pDemand:
Capacity charge on the heat pump's electrical power, in € per kW and year.
Only set it if your electricity price does not already include it. Industrial grid capacity charges are often 50–150 €/kW per year.
Cost = p_L · Q / COP.
input_help.specCost:
Investment per kW of heat output, in €/kW. Linked to the investment next to it: I = c_spec · Q.
Literature: about 200–1.500 €/kW; Danish Energy Agency 2026: 1.400 €/kW up to 125 °C, 1.750 €/kW up to 150 °C (steam, incl. installation). Sources: see the bulb next to the title.
input_help.fMaint:
Maintenance and repair per year, as a share of the investment, in %.
5 % as on the slides; VDI 2067 gives 1–3 % for maintenance plus inspection for heat pumps, depending on the component.
input_help.reinvestShare:
A reinvestment during the period, as a share of the investment, in %, e.g. a compressor overhaul. 0 = none.
It is paid once, in the year below, and discounted like any cash flow.
input_help.reinvestYear:
Year of operation in which the reinvestment above is paid.
Only used if the reinvestment share is above 0.
input_help.life:
Service life of the heat pump, in years, for the residual value (VDI 2067: about 18–20 years).
After T years the plant is still worth I · (1 − T / L) (linear depreciation); that value counts in the net present value, not in the payback. 0 = no residual value.
input_help.funding:
Share of the investment paid by a funding programme, in %. A one-off grant on the investment: (1 − φ) · I.
EEW Module 4 (premium funding) can fund industrial heat pumps; 35 % is the example on the slides.
input_help.coolShare:
Share of the heat source that is actively cooled today, in %.
The heat pump takes heat out of the source, so that part no longer needs cooling. 0 % if the waste heat just leaves (e.g. exhaust air up the stack, as at Hipp); 100 % if a chiller or cooling tower removes all of it today.
input_help.eer:
Cooling COP (also called EER) of the cooling that removes the source heat today: heat removed [kW] / electricity [kW]. It is the cooling counterpart of the heat pump COP; for the same machine, heating COP = cooling COP + 1.
Compression chiller 3–5, dry cooler 10–30, wet cooling tower 15–40 (only fans and pumps). Datasheets in BTU/Wh: divide by 3,41. Only used if the cooled share is above 0 %.
Saved electricity = Q_source · h · share / COP_cooling. Example: 296 kW, 100 %, COP 4 → 74 kW → about 648 MWh/year → about 84.000 €/year at 13 ct.
input_help.opFunding:
Operating funding: paid per MWh of heat the heat pump delivers, lowering its yearly operating costs.
BEW Module 4 pays this for heat pumps feeding heat networks, up to about 92 €/MWh depending on electricity price and SCOP. 0 = none.
Per year: f_B · Q · h, for the years below.
input_help.opFundingYears: Number of years the operating funding is paid, counted from the first year of operation. BEW Module 4: 10 years.

economics.reset_hint: Restore all inputs and investments to their starting values
economics.sens_explain: At a {{fuel}} price of {{pf}} ct/kWh, the heat pump pays off as long as electricity costs less than {{pe}} ct/kWh. That is the dashed line.
economics.sens_never: At a {{fuel}} price of {{pf}} ct/kWh the heat pump does not pay off against the {{ref}}, whatever the electricity price.
economics.sens_help:
Each cell is one pair of prices: {{fuel}} price across, electricity price down, with the net present value written in it. Green cells: the heat pump earns money over {{T}} years (net present value above 0); red cells: the {{ref}} is cheaper.
The dashed line is the break-even: there the heat pump and the {{ref}} cost exactly the same over {{T}} years. It slopes because a higher {{fuel}} price makes the {{ref}} dearer, so the heat pump can afford dearer electricity and still win.
The dot is the prices you entered: the further it sits inside the green, the safer the investment against price changes.
Hover over a cell or the line for the exact values; click to use that price pair in the table and charts.

summary.title: Summary
summary.coverage: This heat pump delivers {{q}} kW of the {{qref}} kW demand ({{pct}} %) at a COP of {{cop}}, drawing {{qsrc}} kW from the heat source.
summary.rest: The rest of the demand stays on the {{ref}}.
summary.energy: It replaces {{fuelKwh}} kWh/year of {{fuel}} with {{el}} kWh/year of electricity, saving {{saving}} kWh/year of final energy and {{co2}} t CO₂ per year.
summary.cooling: It also takes {{kwh}} kWh/year of electricity off the existing cooling.
summary.saving_pos: In the first year it lowers operating costs by {{eur}}.
summary.saving_neg: In the first year it raises operating costs by {{eur}}.
summary.payback_never: It does not pay back within {{years}} years.
summary.npv_pos: Over {{T}} years it earns {{eur}} in today's money (net present value, incl. {{rv}} residual value).
summary.npv_neg: Over {{T}} years it loses {{eur}} in today's money (net present value, incl. {{rv}} residual value).
summary.be: At {{pf}} ct/kWh for {{fuel}}, it stays profitable as long as electricity costs less than {{pe}} ct/kWh.
summary.be_never: It cannot beat the {{ref}} at any electricity price with today's fuel price.

economics.size_click: Each point is the best heat pump of that size on the optimisation curve. Click a point to analyse that pump above.
economics.size_help:
A smaller heat pump sits lower on the sink profile: it covers less of the demand, but over a smaller temperature lift, so its COP is higher and it costs less. The heat it does not cover still comes from the {{ref}}, and that fuel is counted.
The curve is the net present value of every working heat pump from the optimisation, costed with the inputs above; at each size only the best machine is shown. Its highest point (the gold diamond) is the economic optimum: the size that earns the most over the period.
The investment is the specific investment (€/kW) times the heat output for every size. In reality small units cost more per kW, so the optimum may sit at a somewhat larger size.

pinch.pinch: With a minimum temperature difference of ΔTmin = {{dt}} K between hot and cold streams, the pinch lies at {{T}} °C (shifted temperature).
pinch.recovery: Of the {{hot}} kW the hot streams give off, {{rec}} kW can be recovered by exchanging heat between the process streams themselves.
pinch.utilities: What is left has to come from outside: at least {{qh}} kW of heating above the pinch and {{qc}} kW of cooling below it.
pinch.status_quo: Today the process uses {{h}} kW of heating and {{c}} kW of cooling, so full heat recovery could save {{sh}} kW of heating ({{shp}} %) and {{sc}} kW of cooling ({{scp}} %).
pinch.rule: Rule of the pinch: supply heat only above {{T}} °C and remove heat only below it. A heat pump pays off when it lifts waste heat from below the pinch to above it, which is what the next section looks for.
